appraisal_events.evidence: au moment où je ne sentais plus dans mon cœur aucune raison de bonheur, Saint-Loup entrant, ce fut comme une arrivée de bonté, de gaieté, de vie ... mes larmes d'attendrissement.
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's unannounced arrival pulls the narrator out of his solitary grief over Mme de Stermaria, offering exactly the warmth and companionship he had no reason left to expect.

appraisal_events.evidence: « J'ai raconté à Bloch que tu ne l'aimais pas du tout tant que ça, que tu lui trouvais des vulgarités. Voilà comme je suis, j'aime les situations tranchées », conclut-il d'un air satisfait ... il l'avait trahie ... une affreuse sinuosité ... une expression hideuse de bassesse, presque de bestialité.
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup boasts of having repeated the narrator's private, unflattering opinion of Bloch back to Bloch himself; the narrator reads this as a betrayal of confidence, and Robert's satisfied tone and contorted expression are described in strongly debasing terms.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup's visit rescues him from isolated despair, restoring gaiety and warmth precisely when he had nothing left to hope for that evening.
The narrator admiringly frames this kind of friend's rare, brief gift of companionship as paradoxically affectionate and precious.

The narrator judges Saint-Loup harshly for gratuitously betraying a private confidence to Bloch and boasting of it, describing his satisfied expression as taking on a hideous, almost bestial baseness.
His absolute trust in Saint-Loup's loyalty is broken by the disclosure, leaving him stunned and troubled just as the evening had turned warm.

ambiguities: The narrator explicitly weighs several possible explanations for Saint-Loup's disclosure (unconsciousness, stupidity, a passing bad mood at the narrator, or at Bloch) without settling on one, which bears on how deliberately the diminishment of Saint-Loup should be read.
